chunks: Skin effect and where it matters. The question: What is the skin effect? Where does it come up in TLs?
With steady current (DC), current spreads through the whole thickness of a wire.
As the frequency rises, the current crowds into a thin layer near the surface, and the middle carries almost none. This is the skin effect.
A thinner usable layer means less metal carrying current, so the wire's resistance goes up with frequency. It is a main reason copper loss grows at gigahertz speeds.
Picture a long hallway with a crowd moving along it. When everyone walks slowly, people fill the whole width.
When the crowd rushes, everyone hugs the walls and the middle of the hallway stays empty. The hallway is just as wide, but only the edges are used.
In a wire the cause is not crowding. A changing current builds a changing magnetic field, which pushes current out of the middle toward the surface.
Skin depth falls as 1 over square root of f : a straight line of slope minus 1/2 on log-log axes. The horizontal red line is 1 oz copper thickness (35 µm).
Where the copper curve falls to half of that, about 14 megahertz, the conductor starts to behave as a surface layer, and above that you're paying the square root of f penalty.
All four metals are within about 30% of each other (δ scales as √ρ), so the metal choice barely matters; the surface smoothness and plating do.
Skin depth ( delta ): how deep into the metal most of the current flows. It shrinks as frequency rises.
Eddy currents: small circling currents the changing magnetic field creates inside the metal. They cancel current in the middle.
AC resistance: a wire's effective resistance at high frequency, higher than its DC value.
Conductor loss: signal energy lost as heat in the copper ("TL loss and distortion sources").
Surface roughness: tiny bumps on the copper that lengthen the path current takes, so loss rises further.
For copper, the skin depth is about 66 micro m over square root of f over MHz . That is 66 µm at 1 megahertz, about 6. 6 µm at 100 megahertz, and about 2. 1 µm at 1 gigahertz.
A typical circuit-board trace is 35 µm thick. Above about 14 megahertz the skin is thinner than half the trace, so the middle goes unused.
From 100 megahertz to 1 gigahertz the skin gets about three times thinner, so the resistance rises about three times. That is the whole idea.
"The skin effect is high-frequency current crowding into a thin layer at the surface of a conductor.
Induced eddy currents oppose current in the middle and reinforce it at the edges.
The skin depth is delta equals square root of over pi f micro : 66 µm at 1 megahertz for copper, 2. 1 µm at 1 gigahertz.
Since the effective area shrinks, resistance rises as square root of f .
In transmission lines it's the dominant conductor loss: R' and attenuation grow as square root of f , current hugs the surfaces facing the plane, and roughness makes it worse."
